documents.title: Academic Integrity - University Catalog
documents.stance_why: AI appears only as a form of cheating and plagiarism: "work generated through unsanctioned and/or undocumented artificial intelligence (A.I.) assistance" and AI text generators used "without both the explicit permission of the instructor and complete attribution". AI is therefore banned unless the instructor permits it and it is cited, which is a restrict default rather than delegation to instructors alone.
documents.summary: The catalog's undergraduate and graduate integrity standards add AI to the definitions of cheating and plagiarism: AI doing central assignment work requires instructor permission plus full attribution. Instructors are told to say in the syllabus when AI may be used; graduate students must check tools with instructors and cite them.

units.why: Lists AI under cheating: "work generated through unsanctioned and/or undocumented artificial intelligence (A.I.) assistance" is a violation. It binds students and classifies AI misuse as misconduct (P36), not a stance default; the permission/citation rules are coded separately.
units.anchor: work generated through unsanctioned and/or undocumented artificial intelligence (A.I.) assistance.

units.why: The plagiarism definition says "using the assistance of artificial intelligence (A.I.) text generators to perform central requirements of an assignment" is plagiarism. This forbids having AI produce core work (reading, writing, coding) that is submitted, so P19 fits better than P36, which is coded separately for the cheating clause.
units.anchor: artificial intelligence (A.I.) text generators to perform central requirements of an assignment
units.policy: Using AI text generators to perform central requirements of an assignment (reading, synthesizing, interpreting, writing, coding, programming) counts as plagiarism unless the instructor explicitly permits it and AI-assisted components are fully attributed and cited.

units.why: The same sentence conditions any such use on "the explicit permission of the instructor", so AI is off unless the instructor allows it; this is a default-prohibited-unless-allowed fallback (P06), and it also delegates permission to the instructor.
units.anchor: without both the explicit permission of the instructor and complete attribution and citation
units.policy: AI use for central assignment requirements requires the explicit permission of the instructor.

units.why: Requires "complete attribution and citation of A.I. assisted components" whenever AI is used for central requirements. It is an attribution duty on students, so P24 (disclose/cite AI use) fits rather than P25, as no tool/prompt details are specified.
units.anchor: complete attribution and citation of A.I. assisted components
units.policy: Students give complete attribution and citation of AI-assisted components of their work.

units.why: The faculty-roles section says the syllabus "should also mention course policy regarding academic integrity" including "when, if ever, can artificial intelligence tools be used". This asks instructors to state AI expectations in the syllabus (P09).
units.anchor: when, if ever, can artificial intelligence tools be used, etc.
units.policy: The syllabus should state course policy regarding academic integrity, including when, if ever, artificial intelligence tools can be used.

units.why: The graduate standards add that it is "the student's responsibility to discuss tools and resources with course instructors, advisors, and departments before use unless explicitly authorized". Sitting beside the AI cheating clause, it tells students to ask before using tools such as AI (P10).
units.anchor: responsibility to discuss tools and resources with course instructors, advisors, and departments before use
units.policy: It is the student's responsibility to discuss tools and resources with course instructors, advisors, and departments before use unless explicitly authorized in advance.

units.why: The same graduate sentence requires students "to appropriately cite all resources and tools used in all academic work". It is a general citation duty that reaches AI tools, so it is coded as disclosure/citation (P24).
units.anchor: to appropriately cite all resources and tools used in all academic work
units.policy: Students appropriately cite all resources and tools used in all academic work.

documents.unit: Center for Digital Innovation in Learning (CDIL)
documents.title: Teaching in an AI World
documents.stance_why: The page sets no student rule; it says it is "not intended to serve as an official BC policy" and recommends faculty decide through "Purposeful assignment and assessment design" and "Clear communication with students on the role of AI in your course". The decision is handed to instructors, so delegates.
documents.summary: Faculty guidance from the teaching-technology center that advises against AI detectors and for assessment redesign (process-based, AI-resistant outcomes) and open dialogue with students about expectations. It leaves each instructor to choose the AI rules for their course.

units.why: The page says it is "not intended to serve as an official BC policy" but is CDIL's recommendation. This sets the scope and status of the guidance (P56 scope/framework statement).
units.anchor: not intended to serve as an official BC policy

units.why: CDIL recommends "Purposeful assignment and assessment design" as half of a two-fold approach; it asks faculty to redesign assessments in response to AI (P35).
units.anchor: Purposeful assignment and assessment design

units.why: The second half of the approach is "Clear communication with students on the role of AI in your course and a clear explanation for why". This is about communicating the course's AI expectations (P09).
units.anchor: Clear communication with students on the role of AI in your course

units.why: States that detection is "impossible to prove whether or not work has been generated by AI" and that vendors admit "high rate of false positives". This is a statement that detectors are unreliable (P39).
units.anchor: it is impossible to prove whether or not work has been generated by AI

units.why: Notes tools such as Grammarly or text-to-voice "are generally acceptable, increase educational accessibility". This permits long-standing AI writing aids and flags equity; P18 (prose/grammar tools) is chosen over P51 because the rule concerns the acceptability of specific writing tools.
units.anchor: These tools are generally acceptable, increase educational accessibility

units.why: Warns that running student work through AI detection "could inadvertently create concerns regarding FERPA and intellectual property" by putting content in the public domain. It protects student data and IP (P50 over P52, because the issue is data exposure to a tool).
units.anchor: potentially puts their content into the public domain

units.why: States BC "generally does not endorse the use of plagiarism detection software". An institutional position against relying on detectors (P39).
units.anchor: Boston College generally does not endorse the use of plagiarism detection software
units.frag_start: As a result, Boston College generally

units.why: "BC service units will be unable to provide technical assistance or guidance to faculty who independently opt to use plagiarism detection software". This is a consequence of the detector stance and a distinct support limit, still within P39.
units.anchor: BC service units will be unable to provide technical assistance or guidance to faculty

units.why: Says the integrity policy "has been updated (May 2024) to include specific language around the use of AI". It records a revision of policy over time (P54).
units.anchor: updated (May 2024) to include specific language around the use of AI.

units.why: Advises faculty that "Your first goal should be to understand the basics of how it works"; faculty learning about AI before setting policy (P63).
units.anchor: Your first goal should be to understand the basics of how it works

units.why: Advises faculty to "Communicate your expectations in a written statement in your course syllabus and in person". Syllabus statement of AI expectations (P09).
units.anchor: Communicate your expectations
units.policy: Faculty communicate their AI expectations in a written statement in the course syllabus and in person as a facilitated in-class discussion.

units.why: Says to "Facilitate an in-class discussion about GenAI with your students" and calls it "extremely important". No type covers a classroom dialogue separate from the syllabus statement, so it is UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Facilitate an in-class discussion about GenAI with your students.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors hold an ongoing dialogue with students about GenAI in class, beyond the written syllabus statement.

units.why: Reports many faculty believed syllabus statements banned AI, but "students' conceptions about what constitutes an AI tool did not match". This justifies dialogue; no type covers it, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: students' conceptions about what constitutes an AI tool did not match those of faculty members
units.uncovered_note: Evidence that written syllabus bans are not enough because students and faculty define AI tools differently.

units.why: CDIL "has developed a system of visual communication" for explaining expectations on AI for "different assignments". It is a tool for communicating assignment-level AI expectations (P09; P05 not chosen as no named tiers are given in the text).
units.anchor: a system of visual communication
units.frag_end: student use of AI for different assignments.

units.why: Some outcomes "might be AI-agnostic, so you might allow students to use AI freely" while others may not; faculty decide per learning outcome. Permission varies by instructor and assignment (P04).
units.anchor: you might allow students to use AI freely

units.why: Tells faculty to "Design outcomes that require students to meet benchmarks that AI cannot accomplish" such as reflection and teamwork. This is assessment redesign around AI (P35).
units.anchor: Design outcomes that require students to meet benchmarks that AI cannot accomplish.

units.why: States the approach "removes you from evaluating whether students used AI in their work", focusing on meeting expectations alone. Staff do not police AI use; P60 fits best as it states not policing, relying on assessment design.
units.anchor: removes you from evaluating whether students used AI in their work

units.why: Says GenAI "means that faculty need to rethink their assessments away from traditional formats". Assessment redesign around AI (P35).
units.anchor: faculty need to rethink their assessments away from traditional formats

units.why: Recommends process-based and project-based approaches where "the final product is less important than students' ability to articulate their metacognitive awareness". Grading on process is a redesign (P35).
units.anchor: process-based and project-based approaches to learning emphasize students' ability to acquire and demonstrate mastery

units.why: Says a process approach should have "multiple checkpoints for the paper with corresponding feedback sessions". Checkpoints and feedback are part of the redesign (P35).
units.anchor: there should be multiple checkpoints for the paper with corresponding feedback sessions

units.why: Explains that when students see work as busy work "there's a huge temptation to offload this work to GenAI" and that explaining purpose makes them "less likely to feel tempted". It advises making the relevance of tasks clear to reduce AI offloading; P35 as it is assignment design.
units.anchor: if students clearly understand why they are being asked to complete this work

notes: No school-level or CS department policy found; course layer deferred. Cheating and plagiarism AI clauses repeat verbatim in undergraduate and graduate sections; coded once, with graduate-only sentences coded separately. Generic integrity procedures (response to allegations, sanctions) not AI-specific and not coded. Two CDIL units are UNCOVERED (in-class dialogue about AI; syllabus bans insufficient because students define AI tools differently).
